title: Observability onboarding for non-engineering stakeholders
content:
Purpose
This is a short, approachable guide for product managers, customer success, sales engineers, and other non-engineering stakeholders to get comfortable with Redwood Inference observability dashboards and traces. The goal is not to make you an SRE, but to give the right mental model and a pragmatic set of checks you can run when you see a customer ticket or a behavior that looks surprising.

Audience
- PMs investigating user-facing regressions
- CS/SEs preparing for escalations or customer demos
- GTM folks tracking availability/latency SLAs for accounts

Quick-start checklist (3-minute triage)
1) Identify scope: Is this one customer, a cohort, or global? (Check tenant filter at top of the dashboard).
2) Check vanity panels: error rate, p95 latency, and cold-cache rate for the timeframe. If error rate > 1% or p95 latency > 2x baseline → escalate.
3) Look at recent deploys/rollouts and canary tags in the header. If a new model/version rolled out in the last hour, flag for engineering.
4) If the issue is latency, open a trace for a representative request and look at token-first-time vs. KV lookup time.
5) Capture links/screenshots, approximate timestamps, and any customer logs/requests to attach to the ticket.

Key terms (plain language)
- Request: a single user/API call (e.g., a chat turn).
- Token: a generated token; many metrics are per-token or per-request-per-token.
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): how long until the model emits the first token. Good indicator of cold starts or I/O stalls.
- E2E latency: total time a request took from our API gateway to final token response. Use this for SLA comparisons.
- Median/p95/p99: the typical/slow/worst-case latency slices. P95 is a critical SLO signal for user experience.
- Cold-cache event: when the model had to rebuild KV caches (first multi-token request after idle). Cold-cache rate affects latency.
- KV cache warmth: rough percentage of requests that hit a warm cache. Lower warmth → more cold starts.
- Error rate: percentage of requests that returned non-200 or had internal failures (rate-limited, OOM, inference error).

Dashboard sections and what to look for
1) Overview (landing pane)
   - What it shows: global request volume, p95 latency, error rate, and recent deploys.
   - Why it matters: fast glance to see systemic problems (region-wide outage, model regression).
   - Best practice: always set the tenant filter first. Many apparent incidents are tenant-scoped.

2) Latency breakdown
   - Panels: gateway queueing, model-forward-time, token-emission-time, KV-prefetch time.
   - How to read: if token-emission is low but model-forward-time high → CPU/GPU kernel issue; if KV-prefetch jumps → disk/I/O or cache eviction.
   - Actionable signal: sudden jump in gateway queueing suggests throttles or burst traffic; ask SRE for rate-limit configs.

3) Error and retry patterns
   - Panels: error count by type, retry storms, rate-limited responses, OOMs.
   - Look for: correlated spikes across models/regions (indicates infra), or single-tenant spikes (indicates traffic spike or malformed input).

4) KV/Cache health panel
   - What to watch: warmth, eviction rate, TTL saturation.
   - Why CS cares: customers with frequent cold-cache behavior will report choppy latency during demos.

5) Cost/throughput lens (for Dedicated customers)
   - Check token / second and GPU utilization panels. Customers on Dedicated capacity care if throughput approaches reservation limits.

Tracing primer (map to intuition)
- A trace is a timeline for one request. It has spans (segments) representing things like gateway, router, model call, and token emission.
- Use traces to: understand where time is spent, find retries, and find opaque second-order effects (e.g., repeated fetches for embeddings).
- Navigation tips: start from a slow request (p95). Expand spans to see sub-operations. Look for long spans with no downstream activity — those often indicate blocking I/O or waiting for a resource.

Simple investigation recipe (10–30 minutes)
1) Gather: customer request example, timestamp, tenant id, and approximate latency.
2) Reproduce: try a quick local/console call if possible using a short prompt. Note if latency is reproducible.
3) Dashboard checks: overview → latency breakdown → error types → deployment timeline. Save screenshots.
4) Trace dive: pick a slow trace around timestamp, inspect spans for blocking or repeated retries.
5) Annotate ticket: include tenant, graphs, representative trace link, and suggested owner (SRE, serving-runtime, or product).

Do's and Don'ts
- Do: attach trace links and exact timestamps to tickets.
- Do: always check the tenant filter before panicking.
- Don't: escalate to oncall for brief transient spike unless p95 is sustained for >5 minutes or customer impact is confirmed.
- Don't: ask engineering to roll back without attaching data (deploy timestamp, affected model/version).

Example short script to collect artifacts (copy-paste for tickets)
- Tenant: <tenant-id>
- Time window: 2025-02-10T14:02:00Z → 2025-02-10T14:10:00Z
- Observed: p95 latency increased from 420ms → 1.8s; error rate 0.02 → 0.78 in window
- Attachments: screenshot of Overview, latency heatmap, link to sample trace: <trace-link>

Templates you can use (PM/CS)
- Quick status message for GTM: "We observed elevated p95 latency for tenant <id> between 14:02–14:10 UTC. Engineering investigating; initial signal points to increased cold-cache events. I'll update in 20 minutes."
- When to escalate to oncall: sustained p95 > 2x baseline, error rate > 1% for > 10 minutes, or a blocker customer reporting outage.

Privacy & compliance note
- Traces may contain prompt or partial output snippets for debugging. Only share trace links with people who have the right access. For customer-facing notes, redact PII or sensitive content.

Operator notes / things engineers like to see (include these in ticket)
- Exact request id(s) and trace link(s)
- Tenant id and example payload (redact secrets)
- Screenshots of the dashboard with time window set
- Any steps you took to reproduce and whether reproducible

Unresolved questions / TODOs (notes to self)
- Should we add a "non-eng landing" view with plain-language thresholds and a one-click export for ticket attachments? (ask product)
- Quick list of who to ping for Dedicated vs Hosted incidents (make a small contact matrix).

Where to learn more
- Confluence: Observability playbook (linked in top metadata)
- Lunch-and-learn: "How to read traces" session (recording in #ops-observability)
- Walkthrough: book a 30-min shadow with the oncall rotation to see live triage.

If something on the dashboard looks scary and you’re not sure, ping #ops-observability with a screenshot + tenant + timestamp — the oncall rotating team watches that channel and will ask for any missing artifacts.

Document history and ownership
- Created by: Aisha Patel (observability PM)
- Iterations: draft 2024-11-05, update after PM feedback 2025-02-11

End of doc
